title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.1 Problem Statement
The digital revolution has been transformative across the globe, especially in healthcare. This shift from paper-based systems to digital platforms marks a significant change, making healthcare more efficient through the development of responsive health information systems. The adoption of such digital health technologies, although slow, is now seen as crucial for improving public health outcomes, particularly in low and middle-income countries (LMICs), including India. In these regions, the digital transformation signifies a move towards better health management and emergency response. The capacity to collect, analyze, and use health data effectively is key to addressing the health needs of populations faced with limited resources and infrastructural challenges. India, contributing to over 20% of the global healthcare data, demonstrates the immense volume of data generated daily. The country’s efforts to create a digital health ecosystem, highlighted by the creation of over 520 million digital health IDs by February 2024, underscore a commitment to leveraging technology in healthcare.
However, this digital shift introduces several challenges, particularly regarding data privacy, security, and the interoperability of health information systems. Building a robust infrastructure and enhancing the capacity among healthcare professionals are essential steps towards overcoming these obstacles. Despite these hurdles, the transition to digital health systems is essential for delivering more effective healthcare, especially in underserved areas.
The need for LMICs to harness digital health technologies is clear. By developing efficient health information systems, these countries can improve health outcomes and make healthcare more accessible. India’s pioneering efforts in creating a comprehensive digital health ecosystem can serve as a model for other LMICs. Yet, the journey towards a digitized public health landscape is fraught with challenges. The potential rewards of improved healthcare delivery and outcomes are significant, promising a future where technology bridges the gap between traditional practices and modern healthcare needs.
As the healthcare sector navigates the complexities of managing an ever-growing volume of data, it faces the dual challenges of standardization and adaptation. The complexity of healthcare data management, accentuated by the rapid pace of data generation, underscores the critical need for leveraging digital advancements in healthcare. This global move towards digitalization, despite its challenges, holds the promise of a healthier future through improved access to information and more efficient healthcare delivery systems.
The digital revolution has transformed access to information, bringing to light challenges in healthcare data management, especially in low and middle-income countries like India. As healthcare data proliferates, the sector stands at a critical point. The complexity of this data, along with slow standardization and adaptation, forms significant barriers to using digital advancements for improving healthcare.
Despite the rapid generation of data, the digital divide is apparent in areas lacking the infrastructure for digital health technologies. Routine health information systems (RHIS), focused mainly on administrative tasks, fall short in supporting local decision-making critical for meeting specific health needs. The inefficiency of current RHIS is highlighted by their underutilization of data, attributed to technical, organizational, and behavioral challenges. In contexts with complex public health issues, traditional data management approaches are inadequate. This emphasizes the crucial role of grassroots level service providers who need to navigate and interpret data from digital portals like RHIS effectively.
There’s a clear need for decision support tools, indicating the necessity to redesign RHIS to be more attuned to the needs of frontline healthcare workers. Collaboratively designing tools with stakeholders, including medical officers, healthcare providers, and community members, promises more relevant and effective digital health solutions. Enabling local decision-makers to understand and utilize detailed data is vital for improving public health services locally.
Legacy RHIS, with their top-down data aggregation, often lose the detail needed for local health interventions. Health professionals require more specific insights to address their communities’ health needs accurately. This situation calls for a systemic overhaul. Redesigning RHIS to provide detailed feedback and developing decision support tools through participatory methods could empower grassroots medical officers. Such improvements in health information systems would align with global digitalization trends and fill the gap in data utilization for local decision-making. By addressing these issues, there’s a real opportunity to enhance health service delivery for underserved populations, making a significant step towards using digital health to benefit everyone, especially the most vulnerable.
These challenges raise critical questions essential for designing effective interventions to leverage data in improving healthcare outcomes for vulnerable populations. Firstly, it is crucial to understand how data is handled within the healthcare data ecosystem. This understanding involves examining the collection, sharing, and utilization of data across various levels of the healthcare system, from local health workers to policymakers. What methods are used, and how well do they meet the needs and capabilities of these different actors? Secondly, the specific data needs of local decision-makers, such as mid-level program managers, public health professionals, and primary health center medical officers (PHC-MOs), must be identified. These needs are complex, covering not only the types of data necessary for effective decision-making but also the formats and channels that make this data accessible and actionable. The empowerment of these actors is critical, relying on improving their skills in using and interpreting data. This enhancement may require focused training and the development of support systems.
Understanding the structure of the data ecosystem and identifying its key components and actors are essential steps. Knowing who these actors are, their roles, responsibilities, and interactions within the ecosystem, establishes a base for more integrated and effective data-driven strategies.
Moreover, the decision-making processes among these stakeholders deserve attention. Exploring how decisions are made and the role of data in these processes can reveal areas for improvement. Enhancing decision-making might involve creating more intuitive data visualization tools, decision support systems, or better communication channels for sharing insights among stakeholders.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.2 Research Gaps







The digitalization of public health, especially in developing countries, brings both opportunities and challenges. The emergence of new bodies of literature and innovative methodologies suggests a paradigm shift in tackling these issues. The integration of merging methods, which utilize a combination of quantitative and qualitative research approaches, presents a more holistic strategy for understanding and addressing public health challenges.
Participatory methods have emerged as a cornerstone in developing and implementing public health interventions. These methods actively involve the very people who are affected by the issues being studied, ensuring that the solutions are not only relevant but also culturally sensitive and more likely to be accepted by the community. In essence, participatory approaches democratize the process of solution development, allowing for a more nuanced understanding of local needs and challenges. Action Research, in particular, stands out as a study design that promotes the active involvement of stakeholders in the research process. This approach not only facilitates the co-creation of knowledge but also ensures that the solutions developed are grounded in the real-world experiences and needs of those most affected by public health issues. It fosters a dynamic environment where theory and practice continually inform each other, driving meaningful change.
Multiple disciplinary research is another strategy that has seen increasing adoption. Recognizing that public health issues are often complex and multifaceted, these collaborative efforts bring together experts from the fields of healthcare, data science, technology, and social sciences, among others. This interdisciplinary approach facilitates a holistic understanding of problems and leverages diverse expertise to devise innovative solutions.
The push towards data-driven decision-making in public health has been significant. While there has been a concerted effort to harness the power of data for public health, ethical and moral concerns have emerged from across the globe. Some of these issues have been addressed by applying theory and philosophy in the design of digital public health interventions. These philosophical perspectives encourage a reexamination of our approaches, urging us to consider the broader implications of our interventions and to strive for solutions that are not only effective but also ethical and equitable. Incorporating such theoretical frameworks, the Data Science Framework by Harvard University provides a structured approach to leveraging data for impactful decision-making. Similarly, significant reports like the 3D Commission Report on Digital Determinants of Health, the World Bank’s Report on Data for Better Lives, and WHO’s Recommendations on the use of Data from Routine Health Information Systems emphasize the critical role of data in shaping public health strategies. These documents collectively advocate for a systematic use of data to inform policy, improve service delivery, and ultimately enhance health outcomes.
Despite these comprehensive approaches and the newer advances in technology, the translation of these efforts into measurable impacts on the ground remains a challenge. The gap between theoretical advancements and practical application is evident in persistent public health challenges, especially in resource-constrained settings. While there have been improvements in data collection, analysis, and utilization, the anticipated revolution in healthcare delivery, particularly for vulnerable populations, is yet to be fully realized.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.3 Rationale
The digitalization of public health represents a significant shift in how health challenges are addressed, especially in developing countries. This transition offers opportunities for innovative methodologies and a more holistic approach to public health challenges, integrating both quantitative and qualitative research methods.
Participatory methods, placing the affected communities at the heart of solution development, have become a key strategy. These approaches ensure that interventions are culturally sensitive, relevant, and more likely to be embraced by the community. Action Research exemplifies this by promoting stakeholder involvement in the research process, facilitating the co-creation of knowledge, and grounding solutions in the real-world experiences of those most affected. This approach creates a dynamic synergy between theory and practice, driving meaningful change.
Furthermore, the rise of interdisciplinary research acknowledges the complexity of public health issues. By combining expertise from healthcare, data science, technology, and social sciences, this collaborative approach allows for a comprehensive understanding of problems and the development of innovative solutions.
The emphasis on data-driven decision-making in public health has highlighted the importance of ethical considerations. The integration of theoretical and philosophical frameworks, such as the Data Science Framework by Harvard University and significant reports like the 3D Commission Report on Digital Determinants of Health, emphasizes a structured approach to utilizing data for impactful decision-making. These frameworks and reports advocate for the use of data to inform policy, improve service delivery, and enhance health outcomes, addressing ethical and moral concerns in the design of digital public health interventions.
Despite the advancements in technology and methodological approaches, bridging the gap between theoretical progress and practical implementation remains a challenge. The translation of these efforts into tangible impacts on public health, particularly in resource-constrained environments, is an ongoing struggle. While improvements in data collection, analysis, and utilization are evident, the expected revolution in healthcare delivery for vulnerable populations is still in progress. This underscores the need for continued innovation and the application of comprehensive strategies to realize the full potential of digital public health interventions.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.4 Scope of the Study





This study is designed to address the persistent disparities in healthcare services in tribal areas, focusing on Alluri Sitharama Raju (ASR) District, Andhra Pradesh. Despite various data-driven initiatives by the Government of India, gaps in the quality of healthcare services remain. The aim is to harness a data science approach to uncover and understand the barriers to effective data utilization and informed decision-making. Through this understanding, the study seeks to forge tailored solutions that can overcome these challenges.
Central to this endeavor is the transformation of data on reproductive and child health services into actionable evidence for informed decision-making. The participatory action research approach will be pivotal, involving healthcare providers, government officials, community leaders, and the tribal communities themselves. This collaborative method ensures that the solutions developed are not only effective but also resonate with the local context and are sustainable over time.
Moreover, the study plans to utilize the capabilities of data science to sift through large datasets on reproductive and child health services. The analysis will highlight trends and patterns that are not immediately evident, paving the way for evidence-based recommendations. These recommendations are expected to catalyze sustainable improvements in maternal and child health outcomes. An integral part of this process is the development of a user-friendly dashboard. This tool will simplify the access and visualization of data for stakeholders, thereby facilitating informed decision-making and enabling ongoing monitoring of progress.
The analytical framework for this study draws from Deluze’s Assemblage Theory, which views data systems as complex assemblies of diverse elements – including human, technological, and informational components. These elements interact in various ways, contributing to the dynamic nature of health service delivery systems. By decoding these interactions, the study aims to build effective data assemblages that empower local decision-makers. This is particularly crucial in resource-constrained settings, where optimizing health service delivery is of paramount importance.
Ultimately, the scope of this study extends beyond the immediate objective of enhancing maternal and child health (MCH) service delivery at the local level for mid-level program managers. It contributes to a larger vision of creating a global health community that is well-informed, inclusive, and adept at tackling health challenges with agility and resilience. The data-science solutions developed through participatory engagement promise to bring us closer to this goal, marking a significant step forward in the public health domain.

title: 3  Methodology
text:
3.1 Research Context
This chapter provides an overview on the methods employed in the conduct of the study. The chapter is divided into the following headings:
This study was initiated in response to pressing needs within the health system. It actively involved stakeholders from various sectors and levels. The study envisions to co-design and develop contextually relevant solutions to aid mid-level program managers in maternal and child health (MCH) service delivery at the local level.
The core methodology combines Action Research and Data Science to create a robust, context-sensitive framework for co-designing solutions. This approach offers a comprehensive, synergistic strategy that capitalizes on the strengths of each method while addressing their individual limitations. While Action Research excels in generating crucial context-specific insights, it may lack the scalability and capabilities that the data-centric approaches offer. Though the Data Science brings a robust set of tools for enabling researchers to reveal patterns that otherwise might not have been possible through traditional methods alone, it may sometimes overlook the nuanced, complex, and dynamic relationships within a system.
However, on its own, this approach might not ensure that these solutions are adaptable and responsive to the changing digtal public health landscape of the country. Viewing these solutions as Assemblages offer a lens to understand the fluidity and heterogeneity of systems recognising that maternal and child health outcomes are a result of multiple interactions of various actors. This ensures that the designed solutions are deeply rooted in the real-world context, and are both relevant and sustainable.

title: 3  Methodology
text:
3.1.1 Operational Definitions:

Action Research (AR) Action research is a well established research method in the social and medical sciences since the mid-twentieth century, that involves a two-stage process: a collaborative analysis of the social situation by the researcher and the subjects of the research during the diagnostic stage, and collaborative change experiments during the therapeutic stage where changes are introduced and their effects studied.
Data Science Data science is described as an interdisciplinary field that combines domain expertise with statistical, mathematical, and computational methods to extract knowledge and insights from complex data. It integrates domain-specific knowledge with other sciences to inform and guide the analysis, ensuring that outcomes are relevant and applicable to particular real-world contexts, such as healthcare, economics, or environmental science.
Data Science Solution A data science solution in the context of this study is a systematic application of data analysis techniques and tools designed to support medical officers in making informed, timely, and effective on-ground decisions about maternal and child health (MCH).
Assemblage An assemblage is a dynamic configuration of diverse, interconnected components that collectively contribute to a specific function or outcome, retaining their distinct identities while cooperating within a network. This configuration is characterized by its adaptability, the multifaceted relationships among its parts, and its emergence from both local conditions and broader contextual influences.

title: 3  Methodology
text:
3.4 Study Design
To adequately explore the problem, we approached the Administration of the ITDA, Rampachodavaram to discuss the public health problems that they face on a daily basis. Initial discussions led to establishing maternal and child health (MCH) service delivery as the most prioritised issue among others such as malaria, sickle cell anaemia and malnutrition. The ITDA administration provided us with access to the support staff to help us understand the data and issues being faced. Subsequent meetings were set up to plan for the study and obtain the necessary permissions. The draft proposal was then approved by the ITDA administration and ethical clearances from the Institutional Ethics Committee were obtained.
The study employed an Action Research (AR) design based on a Data Science approach. The components of each of these are described below:

3.4.1 Action Research Component
Action Research is focused on solving real-world problems through a cyclical process of planning, acting, observing, and learning. We adopted the cycle originally proposed by (1) and built upon by (2), which have been both major contributions to the field of information systems (IS). For this study, we performed two cycles with the following components: (a) diagnose; (b) plan; (c) act; (d) evaluate; and (e) learn. The specifics of the implementation of these cycles are described in the Study Implementation section.



Components of an Action Research Cycle adopted from (1); (2).




3.4.2 Data Science Component
We adopted the data science framework proposed by (3). The framework starts with the research question, or problem identification, and continues through the following steps: (a) data discovery; data ingestion and governance; data wrangling; fitness-for-use assessment; statistical modeling and analyses; communication and dissemination of results; and ethics review. The specifics of the data science component are mentioned in Section 3.6.3.



Data Science Framework adopted from (3).

title: 3  Methodology
text:
3.5 Study Implementation
The study was implemented based on the action research framework described in the study design section. The research scholar, who is a member of the tribal community belonging to ITDA, Rampachodavaram, took the role of the driver in the change process of co-designing data-science solution.
The first AR cycle was conducted to understand the data utilization and data sources relating to MCH in the ITDA setting, while the second AR cycle was done to design and develop the data science solutions.

3.5.1 Action Research Cycle 1

3.5.1.1 Step 1: Diagnose
In the first stage, we determined the current status of data utilization for local decision-making in the primary healthcare setting of ITDA, Rampachodavaram. We conducted a series of interviews with the medical officers, field staff, and data entry operators to understand the context and actors involved in decision-making. We then examined the current state of activities, data sources, and practices of data utilization, and identified problems, gaps, and needs. We also reviewed the existing data sources and reports to understand the quality and availability of data. The findings from this stage were then used to develop a topic guide for the subsequent stages of the study.


3.5.1.2 Step 2: Plan
A qualitative study was then planned to identifydata sources and explore the prevailing data utilization for decision-making related to MCH in the ITDA, Rampachodavaram setting. Following in-depth consultations with the ITDA administration, three Primary Health Centers (PHCs) - PHC Boduluru, PHC Gangavaram, and PHC Vadapalli - were purposively chosen. The criteria for their selection was the diversity in their local contexts and environments the PHCs represent. PHC - Boduluru and Vadapalli were chosen because of their lack of telecommunication, road and transport connectivity. PHC - Gangavaram was chosen because the medical officer is a member of the community. Topic Guides and additional tools were modified based on the literature review. Also, a subset of the data on MCH services was provided by the ITDA administration which was then taken up for further exploration.


3.5.1.3 Step 3: Act
The study was first piloted in PHC - Boduluru, where necessary methodological adjustments were made based on the initial findings and feedback. The methods included a combination of in-depth interviews, key informant interviews, document reviews, and informal discussions. The study was conducted over a period of several days in both the health facility settings and the field settings. The participants consisted of medical officers, field staff, data entry operators, and other support staff within the health system who play a crucial role in the data lifecycle and decision-making process. The study was then extended to Vadapalli and Gangavaram. Details of the data collection and analysis are described in the Objective-wise Methods section. Additionally, the subset of the data on MCH services provided by the ITDA administration was cleaned and variables of interest were identified.


3.5.1.4 Step 4: Evaluate
The qualitative data was analysed by manual content analysis and themes were organised into three main categories (a) practices, (b) needs, and (c) challenges that each impacted the data utilization of maternal and child health data. The data sources identified were mapped according to the recommendations of the 3D-Commission Report and the findings were then presented to the ITDA administration and the health staff for feedback (torres2021juh?). The data maturity of the health system was evaluated using the Data Maturity Assessment Tool (data.org2022da?). The DMA tool provides a framework for assessing the maturity of data systems in the health sector. The tool was used to assess the data maturity of the health system in three categories (a) purpose, (b) practice, and (c) people. The results were then used to develop a roadmap for improving the data maturity of the health system. The findings were considered baseline data for the subsequent cycles of the study.


3.5.1.5 Step 5: Learn
In this phase, the focus was on integrating feedback from key stakeholders, including medical officers and data operators, to conceptualize a solution addressing identified needs. The deliberation process included perspectives from the medical officers, data entry operators, and data collectors. These deliberations emphasized the development of a data science solution that is tailored to support the decision-making needs at the village/village secretariat level. Additional problems relating to data collection, data quality and data portals were also discussed. Further discussions around the Data Maturity Assessment Tool’s findings informed the creation of targeted improvement roadmaps for each PHC, aligning with the specific contexts and challenges identified through the research.



3.5.2 Action Research Cycle 2

3.5.2.1 Step 1: Diagnose
This stage involved the identification of key variables and inputs for designing solutions based on the needs and challenges identified in the previous cycle. Through comprehensive consultations with the medical officers at each PHC, it was agreed that a customizable dashboard should be developed. Initial efforts centered on creating a prototype with a common layout, which could be adjusted according to the specific requirements of each medical officer. Also, changes in the RCH portal in 2024, including modifications to data structure and user-authentication protocols, necessitated algorithmic adjustments to accommodate these updates. It was also decided that spatial data resources for each PHC must be created for future use.


3.5.2.2 Step 2: Plan
Adaptations to the RCH portal now required medical officers to authenticate access via one-time passwords (OTPs) sent to registered mobile phones. To facilitate efficient data handling, a system of shared folders was established, allowing for daily data downloads post-authentication. This stage involved meticulous review and organization of data sources, with a specific focus on mapping identification variables necessary for data linkage. Concurrently, the attributes for the dashboard were defined, and data pipelines were restructured to align with the recent changes in the data architecture.


3.5.2.3 Step 3: Act
The dashboard’s development adhered to several key design principles, with paramount importance placed on meeting the user’s needs and enhancing data interpretability. Medical officers actively participated in the data exploration phase, collaborating on the creation of data visualizations and summaries. This approach ensured that the dashboard’s design was both practical and user-centric. All data curation, pre-processing, analysis and visualization were done using the statistical programming language R adhering to the best practices in Data Science (3,higgins2022?). Details regarding the development process are elaborated in the Objective-wise Methods section.


3.5.2.4 Step 4: Evaluate
The evaluation phase was conducted in two parts. The first involved testing the functionality and usability of the MCH Dashboard. The usability testing was done through structured sessions with medical officers, where specific tasks were performed to identify challenges and assess functionality. Additionally, impact analysis was carried out through interviews to understand the dashboard’s influence on the decision-making process. For the second part of the evaluation phase, Data Maturity Assessment Tool (data.org2022da?) was reapplied and changes since the baseline assessment were discussed.


3.5.2.5 Step 5: Learn
Structured feedback sessions were organized with all stakeholders involved in the dashboard implementation, focusing on collecting qualitative feedback about the process and its effectiveness. Additionally, Assemblage Theory (buchanan2020assemblage?) was employed as a theoretical framework to analyze how different components of the health system reorganized and interacted throughout the research. This theoretical exploration helped map the connections and dependencies affected by the interventions, providing a nuanced view of the system dynamics.

title: 3  Methodology
text:
3.6 Objective-wise Methods
In this section, we describe the specific methods used to achieve each objectives of the study.
An overview of the study objectives and how they relate to each other is presented in Figure 3.1. Through the first objective, we intend to map the sources of data related to maternal and child health in the study area. Similarly, the second objective was designed to comprehensively understand the data utilization, practices, challenges and needs of the grass-root level functionaries in their daily decision making activities. The theory and wokring hypothesis is developed based on the literature review and domain knowlege. These three elements collectively feed into the third objective. The ultimate aim of the study is to design data science solutions in a participatory way addressing real-world needs and challenges.The lines represent the relationships betweem different element, while the dotted lines represent the components within each element.






Figure 3.1: Overview of the Study Design, the flow of the study is from top to bottom.





3.6.1 Objective 1

Identifying and mapping data sources on MCH care delivery in a tribal setting.

The purpose of identifying and mapping data sources was to provide us with a deeper understanding of the relationships between different elements and concepts in the data. This process was crucial for the subsequent stages of the study, where we needed to understand the data utilization for decision-making. The data sources were identified through literature review, document review, key informant interviews, in-depth interviews and discussions with the stakeholders. Details of the stakeholder engagements are presented in the Study Implementation section. The data sources were then categorised as paper-based vs digital, and traditional vs new/ extended. The data sources were also organised based on seven social determinants of health namely healthcare (H), education (E), access to healthy choices (A), labor/employment (L), transportation (T), housing (H), and income (Y), collectively termed ‘HEALTHY’ determinants as recommended by (torres2021juh?). The data sources were also mapped according to their discovery and repurposing tasks into different types such as designed data, administrative data, opportunity data and procedural data (4). The data are then described based on their category, type, granularity, variables of interest and periodicity. The mapping exercise helped us understand the flow of data from the point of collection to the point of decision-making, and identify the gaps and challenges in data utilization.



Schema for the mapping of data sources



3.6.1.1 Data Source Definitions

Traditional Data Sources These refer to data sources that have already been established and widely used in research. Traditional sources often require institutional arrangements and resources for collection, processing, and dissemination. Examples of traditional data sources in the study include national censuses, surveys, administrative data, and vital registration systems.
New/ Extended Data Sources These refer to emerging data sources that are making new data elements available, often in real-time or on a more frequent basis than traditional sources. Examples of new data sources in the study include social media data, mobile phone data, remote sensing data, and crowd-sourced data. New sources are often more flexible, cost-effective, and timely. However, they may require new analytical tools and their quality and reliability are often uncertain.



3.6.1.2 Based on the Social Determinants of Health(5,6,torres2021juh?)

Healthcare (H) This determinant includes both personal healthcare services (e.g. doctor’s visits) and public healthcare systems. Data sources for healthcare determinants include electronic medical records (EMRs), hospital billing data, and health surveys.
Education (E) This determinant includes primary education, secondary education, and tertiary education. Data sources for education determinants include national censuses, administrative education data, and surveys.
Access to healthy choices (A) This determinant includes access to healthy food options as well as physical activity. Data sources for healthy choice determinants include food security statistics, socio-environmental data, and survey data on physical activity.
Labor/employment (L) This determinant includes employment rate, types of jobs available, and working conditions. Data sources for labor/employment determinants include labor force surveys, employment databases, and administrative data on business establishments.
Transportation (T) This determinant includes availability of public transportation, traffic safety, and access to transportation. Data sources for transportation determinants include transportation databases and patient transportation records.
Housing (H) This determinant includes the overall state of housing, affordability, and safety. Data sources for housing determinants include housing surveys, rental records, and eviction data.
Income (Y) This determinant includes individual and family income levels. Data sources for income determinants include income surveys, tax data, and administrative data on social programs.



3.6.1.3 Based on the Data Science Framework(3,4,7)

Designed Data: Data that have been intentionally collected through statistically designed and structured observational methods for specific research or scientific purposes.



Administrative Data: Data collected for the routine administration of an organization or program, often involving government or corporate operations, without primary intent for research use.



Opportunity Data: Data generated continuously through interactions with digital platforms and services as society engages with technology daily.



Procedural Data: Data focused on documenting the processes, policies, and required standards associated with data handling and management in various contexts.






3.6.2 Objective 2

Understanding the current state of data use, practices and challenges in the primary health centre (PHC) level.


3.6.2.1 Study Design and Setting
For achieving this objective, we conducted a facility based qualitative study within an action research framework, aimed at understanding the data utilization practices in maternal and child health (MCH) services within ITDA, Rampachodavaram. The study was conducted as part of the first cycle of the Action Research. The qualitative approach allowed for an in-depth understanding of the contextual realities while providing the flexibility to engage with the stakeholders in identifying hidden themes and patterns.
The study had two parts: (a) understanding the data utilization practices and challenges in the PHCs, and (b) assessment of data maturity in the organization using the Data Maturity Assessment Tool (8).


3.6.2.2 Sample Selection
As of September 2021, ITDA, Rampachodavaram has a total of 18 Primary Health Centres (PHCs) catering to the health needs of the tribal population. There were 38 sanctioned positions of medical officers, out of which 11 were vacant. Due to the geographic distribution and logistical purpose, it was decided in consensus with the ITDA Administration and the health department that three PHCs will be chosen for the conduct of this study. The three PHCs were PHC Boduluru, PHC Gangavaram, and PHC Vadapalli. There were a total of 5 medical officers, 15 field staff, 3 data entry operators, and 5 support staff in these PHCs. The participants were chosen based on their role in the data lifecycle and decision-making process.


3.6.2.3 Data Collection
For the first part understanding the data sources and data flow in the PHCs, data was collected through in-depth interviews, key informant interviews, document reviews, and informal discussions. The topic guide for these interviews are included in the Appendix. The data collection was done in the local language and the responses were audio recorded verbatim.
For the second part, the medical officers were requested to take the Data Maturity Assessment (8). The self-administered tool consists of 35 questions in three categories (a) purpose, (b) practice, and (c) people and takes 12 minutes to complete. This tool was applied at two time points - baseline and post-test to understand the changes in data maturity.



Data Maturity Assessment Tool (8)


The data collection was done with the consent of the participants and the ethical guidelines were followed throughout the process.


3.6.2.4 Data Analysis
The recorded interviews were transcribed verbatim and translated into English. The transcripts were then subjected to manual content analysis using inductive and deductive coding which yielded codes and categories. The coding was done by two independent coders and any conflicting issues were resolved by discussions. The codes and categories were then reviewed by the research team and the final themes were identified and presented to the stakeholders for validation. The emergent themes were then reviewed and interpreted in the context of existing literature and the specific objectives of the study to draw meaningful conclusions about the state of MCH data utilization and areas for improvement. These were then used to inform the second cycle of the Action Research where the data science solutions were designed and developed.
Additionally, the Data Maturity Assessment was scored based on the responses of the participant. Each of the sub-categories are scored from 0 to 10 which are then used to calculate the categories score and overall score, which are also scored against a maximum of 10. These scores indicate the position of the organization in the journey towards data maturity (See Figure 3.2). These scores were then compared between the baseline and post-test to understand the changes in data maturity. The findings of the study were then used to develop a roadmap for improving the data maturity of the health system.






Figure 3.2: Scoring of the DMA Tool







3.6.3 Objective 3

3.6.3.1 Problem Identification
The data science process started with the identification of the problem. An in-depth analysis of the problem involving literature review, and application of relevant theories was done to find best practices to approach the problem. The role of the stakeholders was critical to bringing data to bear on real problems.


3.6.3.2 Data Discovery
Data discovery is the identification of potential data sources that could be related to the specific topic of interest with a focus on massive repurposing of existing data. The discovery process was critical in outlining the pipelines and associated tools necessary to develop solutions. The discovery started with assembling a list of data sources that are used for local decision-making. The data sources were then screened to include the most relevant variables of interest.


3.6.3.3 Data Governance
Data governance is the establishment of and adherence to rules and procedures regarding data access, dissemination, and destruction. In our data science framework, access to and management of data sources was defined in consultation with the stakeholders, the administration of ITDA and the institutional review board. The data ingestion process involved designing data analysis pipelines that efficiently manages computationally demanding analysis projects by skipping the execution of tasks that are already up to date and supports implicit parallel computing. This functionality ensures that the results remain consistent with the current code and data, enhancing trustworthiness and reproducibility. secure and encrypted storage of data in the server of our institute (SCTIMST).


3.6.3.4 Data Preparation
The activities in this phase was aimed at integrating data from different sources to create a unified dataset that was both comprehensive and suitable for analysis. These activities were done iteratively involving incremental but continuous refinement of the algorithms to address issues of data representativeness, accuracy, completeness, and consistency. All the steps performed in this phase were done using the open-source statistical programming language R (rcoreteam2023?).
The specific steps in this phase include the following:

Data Pipeline Setup The identified data sources were integrated into a data pipeline that facilitated the flow of data from the source to the analysis stage. After thorough literature review and considering the volume and variety of data sources, a computational and reproducible data analysis pipeline framework and a functional programming approach was adopted. This was achieved using the targets package which provides a Make-like environment for computationally intensive tasks in R.(landau2021targets?)
Data Cleaning Once the data is loaded into the pipeline, the data cleaning process was based on the Tidy Data Principles.(9,wickham2014jss?,wickham2019welcome?,wickham2016r?)
Data Encryption In this study, data anonymization and encryption were implemented to ensure the privacy and security of sensitive maternal and child health data. We utilized the encryptr (10) R package, which employs the Rivest–Shamir–Adleman (RSA) encryption algorithm – a public-key cryptosystem beneficial for its security features that rely on the computational difficulty of factoring the product of two large prime numbers.(11) The encryption process involved generating a pair of encryption keys which are stored securely for subsequent encryption and decryption processes. Sensitive fields such as mother’s, father’s or the child’s names, their home addresses, bank details, and contact information were encrypted using the public key, rendering the data anonymous while stored and analyzed. The decryption process, executed only for authorized data validation, utilized the corresponding private key to revert the encrypted data to its original form. This approach ensured that personal data remained secure throughout the study, adhering to ethical standards for data privacy.
Data Linkages In this study, comprehensive data linkages were established between various health data sources to enable a multifaceted analysis of maternal and child health across different administrative levels. The primary data sources integrated were the Reproductive and Child Health (RCH) Portal Data, Health Management Information System (HMIS) Portal Data, and various administrative datasets. To facilitate the linkage of these diverse data sources, spatial data science methods including GIS were employed to geo-reference the data. This enabled the alignment of individual-level data from the RCH Portal with facility-level data from the HMIS Portal and broader administrative-level data. New spatial resources such as the PHC boundaries and Sub-center boundaries were creating using methods for estimating health facility catchment area (HFCA).(12) The creation of these new data resources allowed us to spatial analysis and for visualizing the geographic distribution of health services and outcomes
Data Transformation Following georeferencing and linkage of data, we proceeded with the transformation of the integrated dataset to refine, append and create new variables essential for our analysis. These variables include socio-demographic details, pooled estimates of health indicators, population adjusted estimates, vaccination coverage, categorization of numeric variables etc. This process was executed using R, leveraging the tidyverse suite of packages.



3.6.3.5 Fitness-for-Use Assessment
The unified dataset underwent a rigorous fitness-for-use assessment to evaluate its adequacy for answering the research questions. This was done using data validation checks. The data validation pipeline utilised the principles of Information Management and implemented using the pointblank package in R.(13)


3.6.3.6 Data Interpretation
To adequately interpret the data we adopted the lifecourse approach to maternal and child health. This way we could explore events relating to the lifecourse that are captured through the routine health information system. The data interpretation included exploring the insights into health service delivery like registrations, antenatal care (ANC) visits, postnatal care (PNC) visits, and immunization. This was done thorough a series of iterative processes involving exploratory data analysis (EDA), exploratory spatial data analysis (ESDA) and statistical analysis and modeling.
The findings of these processes are then tabularized and visualised at different levels to facilitate discussion among stakeholders.

3.6.3.6.1 Exploratory Data Analysis
The exploratory data analysis (EDA) was conducted to understand the structure of the data, identify patterns, and detect anomalies. The EDA involved the use of descriptive statistics, data visualization, and hypothesis testing to explore the relationships between variables. The EDA was instrumental in identifying data quality issues, such as missing values, outliers, and inconsistencies, which were subsequently addressed in the data cleaning phase iteratively.


3.6.3.6.2 Exploratory Spatial Data Analysis
The exploratory spatial data analysis (ESDA) was conducted to understand the spatial distribution of health services and outcomes in the study area. The ESDA involved the use of spatial statistics, geovisualization, and spatial autocorrelation analysis to explore the spatial patterns and relationships between health services and outcomes. The ESDA was instrumental in identifying spatial clusters, hotspots, and spatial disparities in health services and outcomes, which were subsequently addressed in the data transformation phase iteratively.


3.6.3.6.3 Statistical Analysis and Modeling
The statistical analysis and modeling were conducted to explore the relationships between variables, identify predictors of health services and outcomes, and develop predictive models.




3.6.3.7 Communication and Dissemination
The study’s findings were effectively communicated through various internal and external channels. Internally, detailed results were presented to PHC medical officers and the ITDA administration during dedicated health staff meetings, accompanied by comprehensive dashboards, presentations and reports that highlighted key issues. Additionally, we organized capacity-building programs to ensure that the stakeholders could practically apply the study’s outputs and deliverables. These programs included sharing well-documented code, data, and operational manuals to facilitate ongoing utilization and understanding.
Externally, the research outcomes were shared with the broader academic community through publications in peer-reviewed journals and presentations at relevant conferences. An open communication channel was maintained throughout the project with all stakeholders, including medical officers and administrative bodies at the district and state levels, ensuring continuous feedback and engagement.

This study was conducted after obtaining ethical clearance from the Institutional Ethics Committee of the Sree Chitra Tirunal Institute for Medical Sciences and Technology (SCTIMST), Trivandrum (IEC Approval Certificate number: IEC/2047; IEC/IECRegNo.ECR/189/Inst/KL/2013/RR-16).

Futher, necessary permissions for data use were obtained from the Administraton of Integrated Tribal Development Agency (ITDA), Rampachodavaram (ITDA Permissions - Annexure Number: ). Privacy and Confidentiality of the data from the RCH Portal was maintained using two factor data encryption and decryption methods. The data was stored in a local disk and access was restricted to the research team.
The study was also registered with the Clinical Trials Registry of India (CTRI) (CTRI/2024/04/066298).

title: 4  Results
text:
4.1
The results of the study are presented as per the objectives of the study.

title: 4  Results
text: 4.2 title: “Untitled”

title: 4  Results
text:
5.1 Data Entry and Collection
Across all three PHCs, data entry processes are largely delegated to frontline staff—namely ANMs, MPHEOs, and data entry operators. Medical Officers primarily receive post-entry summaries rather than directly entering data into systems. Despite the existence of structured portals like RCH and ANMOL, much of the initial data collection still happens manually, particularly in tribal areas where connectivity and mobility are limited.

“Digitalization is a very big problem in the tribal areas. Every data is being collected manually and then they will have to digitalize.” — Medical Officer, Vadapalli


“It’s already consolidated… entered by ANM, ASHAs, MPHEOs… They will consolidate and give us the information.” — Medical Officer, Vadapalli

Though some officers expressed interest in being more hands-on, logistical constraints and legacy practices kept them at a remove from data entry, highlighting a fragmented assemblage of human actors and digital systems.

title: 4  Results
text:
5.2 Data Access
Medical Officers across the PHCs faced structural barriers to direct access, particularly to patient-level or line-listed data. Until recently, many lacked their own login credentials for portals like RCH. Access was mediated through other personnel (e.g., Peter at the district level), or through unofficial sources like WhatsApp groups. Even after being granted access, officers encountered usability barriers such as OTP authentication tied to specific mobile numbers, and the absence of easy filtering features.

“Now a medical officer has been given a RCH ID… I still haven’t opened it. I just received the mail ID and password now in the morning.” — Medical Officer, Vadapalli


“Earlier it was sub-district… now it is each PHC, a separate login ID… separate mobile number for OTP.” — Medical Officer, Vadapalli


“We don’t have access to everything that Peter keeps.” — Medical Officer, Vadapalli

Data access, therefore, was more symbolic than functional—data was “available,” but not readily actionable by those in clinical leadership roles.

title: 4  Results
text:
5.3 Communication and Coordination
Communication within the PHC and across departments relied heavily on unofficial digital channels such as WhatsApp groups, where Excel sheets were circulated. These informal systems were preferred for their speed and familiarity, despite lacking essential patient identifiers. Interdepartmental coordination (e.g., with ICDS, education, or police) was uneven, with Medical Officers often improvising based on personal relationships rather than systematic protocols.

“Monthly report we are not using RCH as of now… in the excel sheet we will be putting it in the WhatsApp group.” — Medical Officer, Vadapalli


“Some ANM are putting ANMO globally… but on and on it is not so… and they want to change that… but they don’t have any control.” — Medical Officer, Gangavaram

This reliance on ad-hoc coordination structures further complicates any standardized, scalable approach to data utilization.

title: 4  Results
text:
5.4 Data Tracking and Monitoring
Data use was largely episodic and compliance-driven. Officers used data primarily to prepare for Performance Oversight (PO) meetings, rather than for real-time monitoring or planning. They lacked tools to track pending cases across categories like immunization, ANC follow-up, or PNC visits. Even when reports were generated, they often lacked line listings or were non-interactive.

“We already have everything. We will put everything into place in that day [for PO meetings].” — Medical Officer, Vadapalli


“If they tell you which are pending, then you can say that this is done… and so he can recalculate.” — Medical Officer, Gangavaram

This reflects a form of reactive data practice, where information is used to answer to higher authorities, not to guide day-to-day clinical or public health decisions.

title: 4  Results
text:
5.5 Connectivity and Accessibility
Connectivity emerged as a foundational constraint, shaping when and how data could be uploaded, accessed, or updated. Both PHC Boduluru and Vadapalli reported significant challenges in mobile and internet access, especially during field visits. These infrastructural limitations fed into broader delays in data entry, validation, and feedback cycles.

“There is no signal in the field… we just note it down and update when we return.” — Paraphrased insight from multiple PHCs


“We need to take someone else’s help to segregate it and then allot it to someone else.” — Medical Officer, Vadapalli

These disruptions extend beyond inconvenience—they reflect structural deterritorializations in the data assemblage that prevent continuity between service delivery and digital reporting.

title: 4  Results
text:
5.6 Staff Engagement and Support
Finally, data utilization was closely linked to staff capacity and comfort with technology. Some Medical Officers and ANMs reported limited orientation to digital systems. One-day orientations were perceived as insufficient, and ongoing support was largely absent. Despite these constraints, there was a visible desire among staff to improve their data-related skills—particularly for task planning, patient follow-up, and decision-making.

“Orientation was for one day… there is no proper information about these portals and applications.” — Medical Officer, Gangavaram


“Actually, we had consolidated reports almost every alternate day.” — Medical Officer, Boduluru

Even when engagement is high, the current systems don’t support staff in building long-term, meaningful data practices that align with their professional judgement or local contextual needs.

5.7 Cross-PHC Comparison
While all three PHCs showed common patterns of constrained and delegated data use, some contextual nuances stood out. In PHC Gangavaram, where the Medical Officer is from the local community, there was slightly more initiative in interpreting data despite low portal comfort. PHC Boduluru reported highly manual systems due to extreme connectivity issues. PHC Vadapalli showed the clearest example of recent shifts—Medical Officers had only just received personal login credentials, indicating a transition stage toward more direct engagement. Across all sites, however, the structural logic of data flow remained the same: fragmented, mediated, and reactive.

title: 4  Results
text:
6.1 1. Portal Usability and System Complexity
A persistent challenge across all PHCs is the cumbersome nature of health data portals such as RCH and ANMOL. Medical Officers described a fragmented access structure, where each PHC has its own login ID linked to a unique mobile number, requiring OTP authentication for each session. Navigating the portals often involves clicking through multiple pages without intuitive design, and the inability to edit or retrieve specific datasets (such as line lists or filtered categories) limits user control.

“No, there is no edit option after we have entered the diagnosis. We will have to send a sample by hook or crook.” — Medical Officer, Vadapalli
“Earlier it was sub-district… now it is each PHC, a separate login ID… separate mobile number for OTP.” — Medical Officer, Vadapalli

The system complexity creates a high barrier to entry for Medical Officers, especially when paired with limited digital training. The portals are not designed for real-time clinical engagement, but rather appear structured around administrative aggregation—alienating frontline users who require speed, specificity, and minimal friction in urgent contexts.

title: 4  Results
section: 6.2 2. Delayed Access and Lack of Real-Time Decision Support
text:
6.2 2. Delayed Access and Lack of Real-Time Decision Support
PHC teams operate in a data ecosystem characterized by lags and intermediation. Medical Officers often do not have immediate access to relevant data—such as immunization or ANC updates—and instead rely on field staff like ANMs or MPHEOs to supply information. However, these staff are themselves working in disconnected areas, without mobile signal, and must later return to the center to upload data. This delay undermines real-time decision-making, especially in clinical or follow-up scenarios.

“We have no real-time view of pending cases or who is due… We just prepare for PO meetings with whatever we are given.” — Medical Officer, Gangavaram
“The field staff are outside, but the system wants GPS tagging from the field. They cannot do it there due to network issues, so they come back to the center… but then they cannot do fieldwork.” — Medical Officer, Boduluru

This cycle produces a constant tension: either staff are in the field doing service delivery or in the center doing data entry. The lack of synchrony and real-time visibility inhibits prompt responses to urgent needs, weakening the overall service responsiveness of the PHC.

title: 4  Results
text:
6.3 3. Training Gaps and Knowledge Deficits
There is a pervasive sense among staff that the introduction of digital systems was not accompanied by adequate capacity building. Training sessions, where conducted, were often described as superficial, one-day events that focused more on procedures than conceptual clarity or problem-solving. Many officers and field staff learned portal use through informal trial-and-error, often relying on peers rather than institutional support.

“Orientation was for one day… there is no proper information about these portals and applications.” — Medical Officer, Gangavaram
“We just learned by doing… no one showed us how to use filters or get reports.” — Medical Officer, Boduluru “No one explained the logic behind the indicators… we just enter and forward.” — DEO, Vadapalli

This knowledge vacuum leads to inconsistent practices, incomplete entries, and low confidence in using data proactively for local-level planning or clinical improvement.

title: 4  Results
text:
6.4 4. Connectivity and Infrastructure Limitations
The technological backbone necessary for digital data work remains underdeveloped in many tribal PHCs. Poor or non-existent mobile network access in field areas means that real-time data entry (especially in ANMOL, which requires GPS tagging) is impossible at the point of care. Staff must return to the PHC or a connected zone to upload records, introducing delays and breaking the continuity of care. Additionally, device limitations—shared computers, old smartphones—compound the infrastructural fragility.

“There is no signal in the field… we just note it down and update when we return.” — Medical Officer, Boduluru
“Sometimes the server is down, or the login fails… We delay everything.” — Medical Officer, Vadapalli

These constraints are not just logistical—they produce a persistent structural lag between service delivery and data reflection, weakening trust in the system.

title: 4  Results
text:
6.5 5. Operational Overload and Workflow Conflicts
Medical Officers and support staff are routinely expected to manage multiple demanding tasks: clinical consultations, field supervision, health reporting, interdepartmental coordination, and digital data entry. These competing responsibilities generate friction. For example, GPS-based requirements in ANMOL require field-level presence to record services, but the absence of connectivity means field staff often have to physically return to the PHC to complete data uploads—forcing a trade-off between service provision and documentation.

“We are expected to see OP, check deliveries, supervise field work, and do data… We can’t do everything at once.” — Medical Officer, Gangavaram
“There’s only one computer and many users. So we just wait or skip the data part.” — Medical Officer, Boduluru “Transportation is also an issue. Sometimes we don’t have anyone to go with to the field. That affects whether data gets collected at all.” — Medical Officer, Vadapalli

This misalignment between clinical logic and data system requirements adds cognitive and temporal load, often pushing data entry to the margins.

title: 4  Results
text:
6.6 6. Cultural, Behavioral, and Interdepartmental Misalignments
Behavioral resistance and coordination breakdowns further complicate data-driven care. Medical Officers reported that some ANMs and ASHAs were reluctant or slow to adopt new portal procedures, especially those requiring field-based data capture or digital literacy. In parallel, volunteers were often unresponsive, and intersectoral collaboration with ICDS, education, or village secretariats was inconsistent.

“Some ANMs are still not comfortable with ANMOL. They say it doesn’t work in the field, so they don’t use it much.” — Medical Officer, Gangavaram
“Volunteers are supposed to help, but they are not active… we cannot force them.” — Medical Officer, Gangavaram “We need coordination from all the teams… schools, ICDS, even police sometimes.” — Medical Officer, Vadapalli

These behavioral and institutional mismatches disrupt the feedback loops that make data meaningful and actionable.

title: 4  Results
text:
6.7 7. Data Quality and Integrity Concerns
Finally, concerns about the accuracy, consistency, and trustworthiness of the data itself were widespread. Errors during data entry, failure of synchronization between systems (e.g., ANMOL and RCH), and an absence of validation mechanisms contribute to doubts about the reliability of what is entered and what appears in reports. Medical Officers often lacked a way to verify or correct discrepancies, nor did they receive confirmation that their data was used meaningfully by higher levels.

“The ANMs complain that the ANMOL data is not synchronizing to the RCH portal.” — Medical Officer, Gangavaram
“We don’t know if the numbers are correct… sometimes things disappear from the dashboard.” — Medical Officer, Vadapalli

These issues weaken the perceived value of data work and reduce motivation to maintain rigor in its collection and entry.

title: 4  Results
text:
6.8 Cross-PHC Comparision
While structural barriers to effective data utilization were present across all PHCs, the manifestations of these challenges varied by local context. In PHC Vadapalli, Medical Officers were in a transitional phase—only recently granted access to the RCH portal—yet were expected to respond to real-time performance reviews. In PHC Boduluru, severe connectivity constraints amplified dependence on manual workarounds, while operational burden was high due to limited staff. PHC Gangavaram demonstrated slightly more coordination autonomy, but challenges around training, synchronization issues, and multitasking were deeply felt. Across all sites, digital systems remained non-integrated with clinical workflows, resulting in fragmented, delayed, and burdened data engagement.

Simultaneous demands for OP, supervision, and data entry; manual segregation time-consuming.
One computer for multiple users; time lag leads to skipping data tasks.

Cultural, Behavioral, Interdepartmental Issues

title: 4  Results
text:
7.1 Data Accessibility and Usability
One of the most frequently expressed needs was access to detailed, patient-specific, and task-relevant data. Rather than aggregated numbers shared over WhatsApp or in PDF summaries, Medical Officers described the importance of line-listed data—organized by village, ASHA, or service type—for targeted follow-up and planning. Without this granularity, it is difficult to assign responsibilities, monitor progress, or act proactively.
Additionally, there was a clear demand for simplified user interfaces. Staff reported frustration with the current design of portals like RCH, where essential information is buried within layers of navigation and the reporting formats often do not align with the immediate informational needs at the PHC level.

“We don’t know who are pending and from which Sachivalayam… we need to assign properly.” — Medical Officer, Vadapalli
“Even if they have the data, they don’t know where to enter the data.” — Medical Officer, Boduluru

This subtheme reflects a broader concern that the structure of available data often serves supervisory oversight rather than operational responsiveness.

title: 4  Results
text:
7.2 Real-Time Data Interaction
Staff across all PHCs expressed a strong desire for real-time tools that could alert them to pending services, delays in data entry, or exceptions in service delivery. In the current system, information flows are fragmented and delayed. ANMs and ASHAs often update portals only after returning from the field, leading to a time lag in data visibility.
Real-time interaction was not simply about technological novelty; it was about enabling responsive healthcare. A dashboard or mobile alert system, updated daily, was envisioned as a tool for tracking progress, redistributing tasks, and preparing for supervisory meetings.

“If a dashboard could give alerts via WhatsApp… that would be better than logging in every time.” — Medical Officer, Boduluru

This reflects a broader orientation toward actionable visibility—data that is timely, relevant, and integrated into the work rhythm.

title: 4  Results
text:
7.3 Training and Capacity Building
Despite ongoing digitalization, training remains minimal and episodic. Staff described receiving one-off orientation sessions—often focused more on data entry compliance than on portal navigation, indicator interpretation, or problem-solving strategies.
Grassroots health workers, such as ASHAs and ANMs, face particular challenges. Many of them lack confidence with mobile apps and struggle with synchronization or input errors, especially when working in low-connectivity zones. Respondents called for not just more training, but contextualized, ongoing support that addresses their specific challenges.

“Orientation was for one day… we need training on how to actually manage databases.” — Medical Officer, Boduluru

This subtheme suggests that without investing in the human infrastructure of data systems, digital platforms will remain underutilized or misused.

title: 4  Results
text:
7.4 Infrastructure and Resource Support
Fundamental infrastructural deficits continue to undermine data utilization. Mobile network coverage is inconsistent, especially in PHCs like Boduluru and parts of Vadapalli, where staff must travel back to the PHC or other locations just to synchronize data. These limitations also impact GPS-enabled tasks in ANMOL and delay real-time uploads.
There is also a need for updated devices and support mechanisms to manage high-stakes data demands during official reviews or inspections. Medical Officers described the stress of preparing for performance evaluations without timely access to clean, accurate, or consolidated data.

“Proper telephone signals would make it more helpful for ASHAs.” — Medical Officer, Vadapalli
“If we have the data beforehand, we could improve before even going to the meeting.” — Medical Officer, Boduluru

In this context, basic infrastructure becomes a prerequisite for digital accountability.

title: 4  Results
text:
7.5 Planning and Feedback Mechanism
Respondents repeatedly pointed to the need for better planning tools—daily checklists, service tracking calendars, and automated summaries that could support micro-level monitoring. These tools would allow staff to pace their work, prevent end-of-month backlogs, and respond to emerging service gaps.
In addition to task-oriented tools, participants emphasized the importance of feedback mechanisms that go beyond fault-finding. There was a desire for appreciation, affirmation, and constructive feedback that recognized the constraints under which they work.

“We will have a deadline so that we will be on track.” — Medical Officer, Vadapalli
“Such appreciation is missing… even if it is a small thing.” — Medical Officer, Boduluru

This reveals an emotional and motivational dimension to data work—where recognition reinforces engagement and retention.

title: 4  Results
text:
7.6 Empowerment and Delegation
Several Medical Officers called for more autonomy in interpreting and responding to data. Currently, they often receive pre-filtered or incomplete data, limiting their ability to make decisions based on local priorities. There were also concerns about blurred role boundaries: some felt they were overloaded with data entry responsibilities, while others described how field staff were unclear on what data to capture and how to interpret it.
The need here is twofold: better role clarity and greater decision-making latitude at the PHC level. This subtheme connects directly to broader questions of institutional trust and the decentralization of authority in public health governance.

“We should be able to monitor the work done by the ANMs… and plan accordingly.” — Medical Officer, Boduluru
“We do not know what’s happening at the Anganwadi center… we cannot monitor follow-ups.” — Medical Officer, Vadapalli

This speaks to a structural desire for redistributing data power—from district and state levels, back to the frontlines of care.

title: 4  Results
text:
7.7 Cross-PHC Comparision
Although all three PHCs articulated shared needs for infrastructure, training, and usability improvements, the degree of emphasis and specificity varied. PHC Vadapalli demonstrated a strong demand for real-time tools and delegation systems, reflecting a growing readiness for digital transition. PHC Boduluru focused heavily on infrastructure, planning mechanisms, and practical feedback loops—underscoring how service delivery in disconnected areas relies on local innovation. PHC Gangavaram, while less vocal on workflow systems, placed more emphasis on training and support for grassroots workers. These distinctions suggest that while structural reform is broadly needed, localized tailoring of data solutions will be essential for effectiveness.

title: 5  Discussion
text:
This is the discussion section
Architectural corrections
Learning Health System
ICMR Policy Document on Health Data Management is a Step in the right direction.
NDHM’s Health Data Management Policy is a guidance document across the National Digital Health Ecosystem (NDHE).
Data Re-Use Policy lacking.
Health Facility ID of India
The Ministry of Health & FW has initiated a process for generating National Identification Number for all Health Facilities of India (NIN-2-HFI). NIN will be random but unique 10-digit number within India. In order to identify the geographical location of the health facility, attributes like state, district, taluka, village codes based on MDDS (Meta Data & data Standards) will be attached to NIN initially. More attributes as per requirements can be added as and when such need arises. NIN will be permanent for that Health Facility and all the Health applications will use NIN in their databases to ensure inter-operability among applications.
Trust - Participatory - Transparency - Accountability - Real Solutions for Real Problems
The Data Science Framework is good. but for its applications in public health, it requires to take into account the health system strengthening and capacity building aspect. There is an urgent need for domain experts in the field of public health data science and they need to be equipped with the right skills and empowered with the best practices in the field.
Involvment of stakeholders is paramount For example, when we repurpose the data on maternal and child health for analyses, medical officers can explain underlying factors and trends in the data that may not be apparent without contextual knowledge or domain expertise.
